scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Dancers of the Pyrenees
This is Basque folk dance. Ancient to contemporary.
on_screen: Title card: Basque folk dance · Spain and France · Ancient to contemporary

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition consists of over 400 distinct dances.
Some are ancient ritual dances originally performed only by men, while others are social dances that allow for mixed-gender participation.
The Dantzari Dantza cycle from the Durangaldea region has remained largely unchanged since at least the 19th century.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dances are performed at religious feast days, carnivals, and processions.
Some dances mark the end of a festival cycle, such as the burning of a symbolic effigy.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Technique varies by dance.
Many involve high jumps, double clicks, and high kicks.
Formations include parallel rows, circles, and individual displays.
Watch for Double click, Flag waving.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Open squares, parallel rows, or circles.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary instrumentation is the txistu (a three-holed flute) accompanied by an atabal (drum).
Listen for the txistu, atabal.
The music is defined by the high-pitched, melodic sound of the txistu flute supported by the rhythmic, percussive pulse of the atabal drum.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Patxi eta Batbiru — Basusarri

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes vary by region and dance type.
In the Kaxarranka, the dancer wears a white shirt, white trousers, a red sash, a red neckerchief, and a black tailcoat, while holding a top hat and a flag.
on_screen: Image gallery: 2 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: The tradition is community-based; groups of 'dantzaris' are the primary performers, often led by a 'buruzagi' (captain).
Variants exist across the seven provinces, including the Dantzari Dantza in Biscay, the Sorgin Dantza in Gipuzkoa, and the Lantzeko Ihauteria in Navarra.
Part of the European folk dance family, with specific links to pan-European sword dance traditions.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Some dances are ritualistic and performed only for specific religious or civic events; outsiders should observe with respect.
